title: Multiplication of Vectors — Vector (Cross) Product
notes: **Definition:** The cross product (vector product) of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is a vector $\vec{C} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ whose magnitude is $AB\sin\theta$ and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
**Magnitude:** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors ($0° \leq \theta \leq 180°$).

**Direction — right-hand rule:** Point the fingers of your right hand in the direction of $\vec{A}$, then curl them toward $\vec{B}$. Your thumb points in the direction of $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$. The result is a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
**Unit vector form:** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \, \hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to the plane of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, given by the right-hand rule.

**Case 1 — Parallel vectors ($\theta = 0°$ or $180°$):** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$. Parallel (or anti-parallel) vectors have zero cross product. This is the condition for parallelism: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0 \iff \vec{A} \parallel \vec{B}$.
**Case 2 — Perpendicular vectors ($\theta = 90°$):** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB$ (maximum possible magnitude). Perpendicular vectors produce the largest cross product.

**Non-commutative property:** $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. Reversing the order reverses the direction. The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE, unlike the dot product which is commutative.

**Cross products of unit vectors:** $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k} \times \hat{k} = 0$. Cyclic: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$. Anti-cyclic: $\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$.
**Distributive property:** $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} + \vec{C}) = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} + \vec{A} \times \vec{C}$. The cross product distributes over vector addition.

**Physical applications:** (1) Torque: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$. (2) Magnetic force: $\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$. (3) Angular momentum: $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. (4) Linear velocity: $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$.

**NEB exam focus:** Define the cross product. State the right-hand rule. Calculate cross products of given vectors. Distinguish between dot product (scalar result) and cross product (vector result). Solve torque and magnetic force problems.

**Comparison with dot product:** Dot product: $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$ (scalar, commutative). Cross product: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \, \hat{n}$ (vector, anti-commutative). The dot product measures
**Geometric interpretation:** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$ equals the AREA of the parallelogram formed by $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. The direction of the cross product is normal to this parallelogram.

**Cross product and motion:** If $\vec{v}$ is the velocity and $\vec{r}$ is the position vector, then $\vec{r} \times \vec{v}$ is twice the areal velocity (area swept per unit time). This is the basis of Kepler's second law.

**Scalar triple product:** $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C})$ gives the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors. It is cyclic: $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = \vec{B} \cdot (\vec{C} \times \vec{A}) = \vec{C} \cdot (\vec{A} \times \vec{B})$.
confusion: ❌ The cross product gives a scalar. ✅ The cross product gives a VECTOR. The result is perpendicular to both input vectors. The dot product gives a scalar; the cross product gives a vector.
❌ $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{B} \times \vec{A}$. ✅ The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. Reversing the order flips the direction by 180°.

❌ The cross product is defined for any number of vectors. ✅ The cross product is defined only for EXACTLY TWO vectors in 3D space. You cannot take $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} \times \vec{C}$ without parentheses — it is not associative.

❌ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ must be zero vectors. ✅ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then either $\vec{A} = 0$, $\vec{B} = 0$, OR $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are PARALLEL. Any one of these conditions makes the cross product zero.

❌ The right-hand rule is arbitrary and any convention works. ✅ The right-hand rule is a CONVENTION, but it must be consistent throughout physics. Using the left-hand rule would flip the sign of torque, angular momentum, and magnetic force, causing contradictions.

❌ $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$. ✅ The cross product is NOT ASSOCIATIVE. In general, $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) \neq (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$. The vector triple product identity is: $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{C})\vec{B} - (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B})\vec{C}$.
❌ The cross product exists in 2D. ✅ The cross product is defined in 3D (and 7D with special structure). In 2D, you can compute a
that gives a scalar ($A_x B_y - A_y B_x$), but this is not a true vector cross product.
practice: Find $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ where $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$. Using the determinant: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(12 - 2) - \hat{j}(8 + 1) + \hat{k}(-4 - 3) = 10\hat{i} - 9\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$.

Show that $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = 6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}$ are parallel using the cross product. $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 4 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{k}(24 - 24) = 0$. Since the cross product is zero, the vectors are parallel. ✓

Find the unit vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(1) - \hat{j}(1) + \hat{k}(1) = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. Magnitude: $\sqrt{1 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{3}$. Unit vector: $\hat{n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

Calculate the torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$ where $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$ m and $\vec{F} = 4\hat{i} - 5\hat{j}$ N. $\vec{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{k}(-10 - 12) = -22\hat{k}$ N·m. The torque is 22 N·m clockwise (into the page).

Find the area of the triangle with vertices at $A(1,0,0)$, $B(0,2,0)$, and $C(0,0,3)$. Vectors: $\vec{AB} = -\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$, $\vec{AC} = -\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}$. $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(6) - \hat{j}(-3) + \hat{k}(2) = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Area = $\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = \frac{\sqrt{49}}{2} = 3.5$ square units.

If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 6\hat{k}$ and $|\vec{A}| = 3$, $|\vec{B}| = 4$, find the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$. $6 = 3 \times 4 \times \sin\theta$. $\sin\theta = 6/12 = 0.5$. $\theta = 30°$ or $150°$. Since the result is $+6\hat{k}$, using the right-hand rule, the angle from $\vec{A}$ to $\vec{B}$ is 30° (counterclockwise looking down the +z axis).
universalFacts: The cross product was independently developed by Josiah Willard Gibbs and Oliver Heaviside in the 1880s as part of their effort to simplify vector calculus for physics applications.
The cross product is unique to three dimensions (and seven dimensions with a special construction). In 3D, it is essential for describing rotation, angular momentum, and magnetic forces.

In computer graphics, the cross product is used to compute surface normals for lighting calculations. The normal vector determines how light reflects off a 3D surface, creating the illusion of depth and texture.
The scalar triple product $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C})$ is used to determine if three vectors are coplanar — if the volume they enclose is zero, the vectors lie in the same plane.
In quantum mechanics, the commutation relation $[x, p_x] = i\hbar$ is analogous to the cross product's anti-commutative property — order matters, and swapping changes the sign.
